titleStmt.title: Sufficient Condition for Real-Time Non-preemptive Scheduling of Interactive Multimedia Tasks

analytic.title: Sufficient Condition for Real-Time Non-preemptive Scheduling of Interactive Multimedia Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In many fields, non-preemptive real-time scheduling of a set of periodic tasks with different release times is very important if not even necessary. The number and characteristics of tasks may vary during time, thus imposing to re-evaluate the task schedulability over time. In this paper we propose an efficient sufficient schedulability condition, and we analytically show that if this bound is satisfied, the tasks are real-time schedulable under the non-preemptive Earliest Deadline First and Rate Monotonic policies. We experimentally analyse, by simulation, the bound and show that in practical cases occurring in Multimedia processing its validity remains significant for a very large range of CPU utilisation factors. In the same way we show by simulation that the gap of the proposed condition to the sufficient and necessary condition is negligible if the difference between the periods of periodic tasks is small. Finally, we give a graphical interpretation of the proposed bound and some application examples.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Interactive videoconference is an example of multimedia system which continuously streams different types of media between users. Such systems must manage the connections of clients using different type of networks and different type of devices. More precisely, each client may be a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop, a fixed videoconference station, a NetTV or a desktop PC. Each type of client can operate at different video/audio resolution. To optimise the bandwidth of the streaming, an adaptation of the stream rate to the clients of the multimedia system is required. In such systems, real time constraints are involved at various levels. For example, at the CPU level, the processing of video and audio frames exchanged among users during a videoconference must be completed before the next frame is acquired. Moreover, at the communication level, the transmission of data coming from different devices at different bit rates must be performed such that the continuity of the stream is preserved.

Real time scheduling of multimedia tasks can be preemptive or non-preemptive. In the first case, only continuity of the stream can be preserved as in case of listen only participants to a multimedia conference, while in the second case it is avoided that an I/O critical operation is interrupted, as in the case of interactive participation to a multimedia conference. In such hard real-time situations a feasibility test must be performed to be sure that the tasks can be executed within their deadlines. The complexity of such feasibility tests plays an important role in real-time systems.

Although most of the existing scheduling algorithms are executed using task preemption, mainly because of its optimality [9], non-preemptive scheduling is often required in communication tasks, in perception tasks and in general in all the tasks where the cost of preemption is too high. However, if on one hand non-preemptive scheduling could introduce large blocking times thus limiting the schedulability of the task set, on the other hand often non-preemptive scheduling is required by the application.
In multimedia processing, non-preemption is required when interaction is introduced.

In this paper we propose a low complexity and efficient condition suited for interactive multimedia streams task scheduling, that assures the feasibility of non-preemptive scheduling of tasks. The contribution of this paper is to propose a sufficient schedulability bound under Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Rate Monotonic (RM) policies. This bound has less computational complexity than the necessary and sufficient conditions presented in [7]. We show that if the bound is used to schedule multimedia interactive tasks, its performances are comparable to that of the optimum bounds. We show that utilisation factor and total idle time depend on the ratio between the shorter and longer task periods.

This paper is organised as follows. In Section II the computational model, the assumptions and previous works are outlined. In Section III we present the sufficient condition for the schedulability of multimedia task set. In Section IV implementation consideration and computational complexity of the proposed bound is discussed. In Section V some simulation results are reported and discussed and in Section VI a multimedia test case is presented. In Section VII some final remarks and conclusions are reported.

div.head: II. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: In multimedia signal processing, the hardware processors can manage many data streams as they use specialised processors to implement some operations.

div.head: A. Computational Model and Assumptions
div.p: A periodic task is denoted by τ i . A periodic task set is represented by the collection of periodic tasks, T = {τ i }. Each τ i is associated with activation time instant (task release time), worst case computation time and period, called (a i , c i , T i ) respectively. The total utilisation of a periodic task set τ is given by U n = n i=1 u i , where u i = ci Ti is the utilisation of task i and n is the number of tasks in T .

A concrete task is defined as a task with a specified release time, or the time of the first invocation. A periodic task set is said to be schedulable if and only if all concrete task sets that can be generated from the periodic task set are schedulable. We will consider only periodic task sets in this paper. The difficulty of scheduling tasks can be affected by the release time.

For a concrete set of tasks, the processor demand in the time interval [a, b] is the maximum amount of processing time required by the tasks in the set in the interval [a, b] to complete execution of all invocations of tasks with deadlines in the interval [a, b].
In the following we give a summary of assumptions used in this paper.
• There is only one processor.
• Scheduling overhead is ignored.
• The relative deadline for each task corresponds to the period.
• Tasks are sorted in non-decreasing order by period. That is, for any pair of tasks τ i and τ j , if j < i then T j ≤ T i .

div.head: B. Previous work
div.p: Scheduling theory has been extensively studied in the last decades for its relevance in practical applications. Scheduling algorithms may be either preemptive or non-preemptive. Each approach has advantages and disadvantages so, in general, the best approach should be chosen on the basis of the particular application.
The main difficulty in non-preemptive scheduling is that it is, in general, an NP-complete problem for every processor load [6].

However, Jeffay et al. in [7] and Georges in [6] show that in certain constrained cases the NP-completeness can be broken. In particular, Jeffay et al. show that necessary and sufficient scheduling conditions for a set of n periodic tasks under nonidling EDF are given by eq. ( 1) and (3), called in the following Jeffay Bound (JB):
div.formula: n i=1 c i T i ≤ 1(1)
c i ≤ L - i-1 j=1 L -1 T j c j(2)
∀ i > 1, ∀ L : T 1 ≤ L ≤ T i where T 1 ≤ T 2 ≤ . . . ≤ T n .
div.p: In other words, informally, the EDF scheduling of the set of n periodic tasks is feasible if, according to the first condition, there is enough computational capacity to execute all the tasks while, according to the second condition, the total computational demand in a temporal interval of length L is less then the length of the interval.

Concerning feasibility, it is worth noticing that, although generally the feasibility of preemptive scheduling is higher than non-preemptive, the overhead is often higher since many unnecessary preemptions may occur during runtime. For this reason many authors have proposed various limited scheduling fixed priority criteria. As it was pointed out by many researchers, limited preemption methods can lead to superior feasibility over fully preemptive and non-preemptive fixed priority scheduling. For example, the deferred preemption model proposed by Burns [5] and analyzed in [1], [4], [8], [11] is a trade off between these two criteria. According to this model, pre-emption can only occur at some given preemption points of the task code so it is deferred when preemption occurs before these points; the number of preemptions can be thus controlled. Wang and Saksena [10] proposed another approach for limiting the preemptions in fixed priority systems. Their method introduces the concept of preemption thresholds. Each task is allowed to preempt only when its priority is higher than the threshold assigned to it. The limited preemption scheduling approach proposed by Baruah in [1] and analysed in [2], [12], is a hybrid scheduling scheme that permits preemption when necessary for feasibility but avoids unnecessary preemptions during runtime. Bertogna et al proposed in [3] another variant of limited preemption strategy considering the non-preemptive execution of selected regions of code of fixed priority task systems.

div.head: B. Graphical interpretation
div.p: We can gain some insight on non-preemptive scheduling by looking at Fig. 1, that is a graphical representation of the CPU time required by each process as time passes. For simplicity all the tasks start in t = 0. The execution times are depicted as vertical lines in the moment of the process' deadline. The The bold line at 45 degree is the total CPU available time and the lines below it represent the processes execution times.
figure describes the notion of task utilisation graphically. The sum of task utilisations, U i , is the angular coefficient of the i-th line.

From the figure it is clear that the task utilisation u i defines the area between lines U i •t and U i-1 •t. If the task is executed, the CPU time it used is inside the slot at the end of period. In order to guarantee enough CPU time it is sufficient for a task τ i to have U i • t < 1. This expresses in another form the first Jeffay condition (eq. ( 1)).

The idea behind SB is to limit the execution times in T 1 as a function of the task utilisation. Fig. 2 shows that this strategy is better than just limiting the overall sum of task's execution times below the smallest period; this obvious bound is called Trivial Bound (TB) in the following. For example, consider the three periodic tasks: τ 1 = (0, 1, 5), τ 2 = (0, 2, 7) and τ 3 = (0, 2.5, 9). Using the Trivial Bound, these tasks are not schedulable as the condition c 1 + c 2 + c 3 ≤ T 1 fails, but using the Slot Bound these tasks are schedulable. By the time the deadline comes, the slot is sufficiently large to accommodate for the execution of the corresponding task.

div.head: IV. IMPLEMENTATION AND COMPLEXITY
div.p: In this Section an efficient implementation of the SB is presented and time computational complexity in terms of elementary CPU operations is considered.
The SB schedulability condition is stated for a single task in the task set. The task set itself is schedulable if and only if all the tasks in the task set are schedulable.
The proposed implementation can be separated in two steps for an easier description: the schedulability test and the update step.

div.head: A. Schedulability test
div.p: The schedulability test uses the SB condition, eq. ( 3), to ascertain schedulability of all the tasks in a taskset.

It is performed after each insertion of new task or modification of an existing task in a taskset. To speed up the calculation, the partial sums U i are stored in memory. Let T new be the new task. U new is computed in the update step by the simple formula U new = U prev + u new where u new = c new /T new , and U prev is taken from the previous task 1 . All the U j with j > new are then incremented by u new .

Let us define the slack of a task τ i as slack i = T 1 -U i-1 • T 1 -c i Let's denote with T ms the task with the minimum slack, i.e. with the highest value of U i-1 • T 1 + c i . From eq. ( 3), it directly follows that if the schedulability test is positive for the task T ms then it is automatically positive for all other tasks in the task set. Therefore if we keep track of the task T ms the schedulability test consists of few elementary operations, i.e. is O(1). The task T ms is tracked by keeping ordered the tasks during the update step.

div.head: B. Update step
div.p: Following the acceptance of the new/modified task or the deletion of a task, the update step is necessary to keep the schedulers' task related data structures updated. In particular it is necessary to maintain the ordering of the tasks such to guarantee efficient O(1) schedulability test. This can be done efficiently with a direct-address table, i.e. by using the period or slack of the new task as a direct index in the table. If the number of keys is small, each task is indexed into the k-th position of the array. The tasks are thus automatically ordered. In order to skip the empty rows of the table a corresponding bitmap is used to indicate which records in the table are not empty. Therefore, an efficient find-first-bit 2 instruction can be executed on a bitmap to find previous and next non empty records in the table. This is similar to many O(1) algorithms which need to find the first non-empty queue signified by an array of bits.

An example of this technique with period used as a key is presented in Fig. 3. 1 Depending on implementation Uprev can be taken either by maintaining a double linked list or using a find-first-bit CPU instruction as explained in the next paragraph describing the update step. 2 Present in all modern CPU architectures. When a universe of all possible keys is very large a multilevel table can be used to reduce memory requirements as depicted in Fig. 4. With a multi level structure, excluding level 0, memory is allocated only for non empty blocks. All the operations of searching, inserting and deleting a record in a direct-address table are O(1). Finding the first, previous and next task in the table can be very efficient, i.e. for bitmaps of limited size they can be executed in constant time by using find-first-bit operations. The addition of the same constant to multiple tasks in order to update the partial sums is not constant time but it can be performed very efficiently as a bulk operation on a contiguous array.

div.head: V. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: In this section the results of extensive simulations are presented comparing the SB to the necessary and sufficient conditions of JB. The gap between the two in different scenarios is studied by looking at the average number of schedulable tasks for each bound. In order to clearly position the bounds these are also compared on one side with the optimal preemptive scheduler (U < 1) which schedules largest number of tasks and the TB on the other, a simple but too stringent condition which schedules least number of tasks.
The average number of scheduled tasks was calculated by considering 1000 random tasksets in each experiment.

A random taskset was generated starting from an empty set and adding one after another random tasks. For random tasks, period and execution times were chosen with uniform probability distribution. First the period, T , uniformly chosen between T min and T max , and then execution time uniformly chosen with c < u max • T . At each addition of a task in a taskset, the CPU utilisation U was checked. The addition of tasks continued while U < 1 in order to maximize the number of scheduled tasks. The generation of one task set was then completed. The procedure was repeated for the next task set. In one experiment 1000 random tasksets were stored in memory and tested against the bounds.
Each experiment was then repeated for different maximum task utilisation u max .

In the first set of experiments shown in Fig. 5 the periods and worst case computation times of the tasks were chosen randomly with the condition that the computation time c is c < u max • T . As expected, the results in Table I show a significant drop of the average number of schedulable tasks with increasing u max . Under these generic conditions the SB schedules some 40% less of the tasks scheduled by JB when u max is small.

In the second set of experiments shown in Fig. 6 the same conditions as before were applied with the additional constraint that T min /T max =1/6. By limiting the relative range of periods we expect the SB to gain some ground compared to JB. In fact the higher the ratio T min /T max , the more similar SB and JB become. In the extreme case of all the tasks having identical periods the SB becomes mathematically equivalent to JB and therefore optimal. In this case the behaviour of the SB is very similar to the optimal JB and the majority (98.4% for u max =0.005) of the tasks are scheduled. The average number of schedulable tasks increased for each bound. The explanation lies in the constraint c < u max • T . With T max constrained to 6 • T min the c on average is not as large as in the first experiment so it is more easily schedulable.

div.head: VI. MULTIMEDIA SCHEDULING TEST CASE
div.p: In the third and final series of experiments we present a case of a multimedia streaming server that is capable of recoding in real-time multimedia streams in several different formats for many clients. In particular it is capable of recoding a multimedia event at different frame rates and using different resolutions and colour spaces. For example it can recode a stream of grey level images, 320x240 pixels, at 5 frame per second or the same stream at 30 frame per second, 1920x1080 pixels and an RGB colour space using 8 bit for each colour.

The multimedia streaming server can dynamically change the number and/or characteristics of the scheduled tasks. The number of tasks changes as new clients connect to multimedia events or existing clients disconnect. The stream that is offered to clients can change dynamically in relation to variations of the system load (available bandwidth and computational load). In this case one or more tasks can be re-scheduled with a different frame rate and/or a different resolution.
The test case is constructed as follows.

There are multiple multimedia events with up to 5 clients connected to a single event. The period of the tasks that stream one event to the participants is given by the required frame rate. In accordance with the example previously mentioned we set the minimum frame rate to 5 frames per second and the maximum frame rate to 30 frames per second. This gives the T min /T max ratio of 1/6. The clients use different devices (smartphone, pc, ...) so the optimal resolution and colour space may vary between clients and with them the maximum computation time of the tasks.

If there is a need to reduce the system load, a task can switch to a lower frame rate or smaller resolution. In both cases u max is reduced. If the opposite is true, the task can switch to a higher frame rate or resolution and u max is increased.

For faster CPU, the worst computation time decreases with smaller u max , the number of tasks that can be scheduled by non-preemptive scheduler increases. In the simulations we study the test case for several different values of u max . 6, but with multiple groups of tasks having same period (5 tasks per group, except last group). The number of schedulable tasks allowed by the Slot Bound proposed in this paper is very close to that of the optimal Jeffay Bound. From these multimedia related experiments, the bound proposed in this paper essentially behaves in the same manner as Jeffay. In particular, for low value of u max the difference is less than 2%. It is evident that the proposed bound is thus preferable than Jeffay since it reduces the CPU cycles.

div.head: VII. FINAL REMARKS AND CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper we propose simple yet efficient sufficient condition for non-preemptive, real-time scheduling using EDF and RM policies. Non-preemption is required in interactive multimedia scenarios and the proposed bound saves computational time to multimedia systems. Experimental results concerning this scenario show that the proposed condition is able to guarantee a subset of feasible tasks very close to what is guaranteed by the optimum conditions.
Future works are related to the implementation on FPGA of the scheduling algorithm proposed, and on the extension of such condition to multiprocessor systems.
